query: For the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni alloy and its equiatomic quaternary and ternary subsets that are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain why their mechanical properties differ during deformation and failure when constituent count alone is inadequate? Specify a controlled comparison, predictions relative to the quinary baseline, the applicable boundary conditions, supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In the equiatomic FCC alloys, the presence of Mn induces magnetic frustration that increases the local variability of stacking fault energies (SFE). This variability delays the nucleation of deformation twins and suppresses the localized fcc-to-hcp transformation. In contrast, Mn‐free or Mn‐reduced subsets (quaternary or ternary) exhibit a more uniform, lower local SFE environment that promotes earlier twin formation and/or fcc-to-hcp transformation, thereby enhancing early strain hardening and delaying crack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Thermomechanically processed, single-phase FCC equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi (quinary) and its respective equiatomic quaternary and ternary derivatives (e.g., CrCoNi and a Mn-free quaternary such as CrFeCoNi) with similar grain sizes and defect densities.
generation.intervention: Perform identical tensile deformation tests (at controlled room and cryogenic temperatures and constant strain rate) with in situ microstructural imaging (TEM) and local chemical/magnetic characterization (e.g. atom probe tomography and/or magnetic measurements) to quantify the onset of deformation twinning and/or localized fcc-to-hcp transformation events.
generation.conditions: Samples must be processed by the same thermomechanical route (e.g., high-pressure torsion plus annealing) to yield similar grain sizes; tests should be carried out under identical strain rates and temperatures (ambient and cryogenic) to isolate the role of local chemical/magnetic variations.
generation.structural_mediator: The local stacking fault energy distribution and the density of twin/hcp phase embryos at defect sites (stacking faults and twin boundaries) mediate the deformation modes.
generation.mechanism: Mn in the quinary alloy introduces magnetic frustration that increases fluctuations in local bonding environments, leading to a wider distribution of SFEs. This higher variability creates a kinetic barrier for the nucleation of twins and the fcc-to-hcp phase transformation, resulting in a delayed activation of these deformation mechanisms. In Mn-free or lower Mn-content alloys, the more uniform SFE landscape permits earlier twinning and/or phase transformation, which in turn enhances work hardening and toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical mechanical loading, the Mn-free (or reduced) quaternary/ternary alloys will exhibit a lower critical strain for the nucleation of twins and/or fcc-to-hcp transformation, a higher early strain hardening rate, and delayed or less pronounced crack propagation compared to the Mn-containing (quinary) CrMnFeCoNi alloy.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy serves as the baseline where magnetic frustration from Mn yields a higher local SFE variability and correspondingly delayed twin/phase transformation onset.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies only to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys processed to similar microstructures under controlled thermomechanical conditions and tested at room and cryogenic temperatures, where magnetic effects on local bonding are significant.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal extends the conclusions drawn by PMC5893566 (which connected Mn-induced magnetic frustration to suppression of the fcc-to-hcp transformation) and PMC5978039 (which observed an earlier onset of twinning in CrCoNi) into a quantitative regime by directly correlating local SFE distributions with twin/phase formation. The uncertainty lies in the precise quantitative role of local SFE fluctuations and magnetic ordering, which has not been measured directly across all subsets.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare three sets of HEA samples – the equiatomic quinary CrMnFeCoNi, a Mn-free ternary (e.g., CrCoNi), and a quaternary alloy (e.g., CrFeCoNi) – using identical thermomechanical processing. Conduct uniaxial tensile tests at room and cryogenic temperatures with in situ TEM imaging and complementary local chemical (e.g., atom probe tomography) and magnetic measurements. Quantify the critical strain for the onset of twin nucleation and any local fcc-to-hcp transformation, and measure the strain hardening rate of each alloy.
measurements: Critical strain at which deformation twins (or hcp embryos) first form
Twin density and extent of fcc-to-hcp transformation as a function of strain
Strain hardening rate from stress–strain curves
Local SFE estimates via computational modeling or indirect experimental probes
Magnetic moment distributions from local measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mn-free (ternary/quaternary) samples do not exhibit a statistically significant earlier onset (beyond experimental uncertainty) of twin or fcc-to-hcp transformation events and do not show higher early strain hardening compared to the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy, then the hypothesis that Mn-induced magnetic frustration and associated SFE variability delays these mechanisms is falsified.

AbstractCrCoNi alloy exhibits a remarkable combination of strength and plastic deformation, even superior to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy. We connect the magnetic and mechanical properties of CrCoNi, via a magnetically tunable phase transformation. While both alloys crystallize as single-phase face-centered-cubic (fcc) solid solutions, we find a distinctly lower-energy phase in CrCoNi alloy with a hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structure. Comparing the magnetic configurations of CrCoNi with those of other equiatomic ternary derivatives of CrMnFeCoNi confirms that magnetically frustrated Mn eliminates the fcc-hcp energy difference. This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy, and is triggered by dislocation slip and interaction with internal boundaries. This phase transformation sets CrCoNi apart from the parent quinary, and its other equiatomic ternary derivatives, and provides a new way for increasing strength without compromising plastic deformation. cited_evidence.text: The deformation behavior of the CrCoNi alloy during HPT processing is very similar when compared to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy []. For both materials, a strong tendency for mechanical twinning during deformation, at least at lower temperatures, is reported in literature [,,,], but the onset of twinning for the CrCoNi alloy should happen at much lower strains as compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy. This also is stated to be one of the reasons for the superior mechanical properties of the CrCoNi alloy, since it leads to an extended strain range with an increased work hardening capacity []. In general, during HPT processing of the CrCoNi alloy the deformation behavior is as expected of a single-phase fcc alloy with low to medium stacking fault energy: For low shear strains, plastic deformation is mostly mediated by dislocation glide and multiplication. For higher shear strains, micro-shear banding, but also mechanical twinning, are activated. A further increase in strain usually leads to an activation of additional twin variants, which results in profuse intersection of twins with different orientations.
